chunks: From him, from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Ulwān, from 'Amr ibn Khālid, from Zayd ibn 'Alī, from his fathers, from 'Alī (peace be upon him) who said:

"The one manumitted on the master's death (mudabbad) is from the one-third [of the estate], and whatever debt he incurs, and the one who enters into a contract of manumission (mukatib), and the mother of the child (umm al-walad), then the master is liable for their debts."

key_terms.أُمُّ الْوَلَدِ: Umm al-walad: A slave mother of her master's child
key_terms.الْمَوْلَى: The master (in this context, referring to the estate/debtor)
key_terms.الْمُعْتَقُ عَلَى دُبُرٍ: Mudabbad: A slave manumitted to take effect upon the master's death
key_terms.الْمُكَاتَبُ: Mukatib: A slave who has contracted to pay a sum for their freedom

ai.seo_question: Who is liable for the debts of a mudabbad, mukatib, and umm al-walad in Shia inheritance law?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that the mudabbad, mukatib, and umm al-walad are treated as debts from the one-third of the estate reserved for bequests, ensuring their manumption or freedom is prioritized. It further establishes the principle of vicarious liability, where the master remains financially responsible for any torts or damages (jinayat) committed by these slaves, reflecting the Shia juristic view on the intersection of property rights and personal liability in manumission cases.
